summary: DMARC lets the owner of an email's Author Domain state how receivers should handle messages that fail validation, and request reports about use of the domain. Receivers can use this when deciding what to do with mail. This Standards Track document obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091.

plainLanguage.summary:
Anyone can put any domain in the From header of an email. DMARC gives the rightful owner of a domain a way to publish, in DNS, what should happen to mail that uses their name but does not check out.

A message passes when the domain that signed it or that sent it matches the domain in the From header. When it does not, the owner's published policy decides: leave it alone, put it aside, or refuse it. The owner also asks to be told, in periodic reports, about the mail that fails, which is how broken sending arrangements get found.

questions: where is the dmarc record published
subtitle: Letting a domain owner say what should happen to email that claims to come from their domain.

tldr.problem: The domain in the From header of an email is easy to forge, and the two existing checks on that domain say nothing about whether the message really came from the owner.
tldr.mechanism: DMARC lets the owner of a domain publish a DNS record that ties the From domain to the result of the existing checks. A message passes only when the domain that authenticated it matches the domain that claims it, either exactly or within the same organisational domain.
tldr.outcome: Receiving servers get a verdict, a pass or a fail, and the owner gets to say what a fail should mean: nothing, quarantine or reject. The owner also gets reports about mail using the domain, which is how most people find out their own sending is broken. The RFC obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091.

facts.label: Policy record location
facts.value: A TXT record at _dmarc plus the domain name

facts.label: Maximum DNS queries in a tree walk

today: RFC 9989 is a Proposed Standard from May 2026. It obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, moving DMARC from an informational document to a Standards Track one, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What DMARC Is For
sections.content:
Abusive email often includes unauthorized and deceptive use of a domain name in the From header field, and the domain typically belongs to an organization expected to be known to, and presumably trusted by, the recipient. The Sender Policy Framework and DomainKeys Identified Mail protocols provide domain-level authentication but are not directly associated with that domain. DMARC leverages these two protocols, giving domain owners a way to publish a DNS text record describing the email authentication policies for their author domain and to request specific handling for messages using that domain that fail validation. Those DNS records are called DMARC policy records.

As with the two underlying protocols, validation results in a verdict of either pass or fail. A pass requires not only a pass verdict for the message but also that the domain associated with it be aligned with the author domain in one of two modes, relaxed or strict. Domains are in relaxed alignment if they have the same organisational domain, which is the domain at the top of the namespace hierarchy for that domain while having the same administrative authority. They are in strict alignment only if they are identical. The choice of mode is left to the domain owner that publishes the policy record.

A pass indicates only that the use of the author domain has been validated for that message as authorized by the owner. Such authorization carries no explicit or implicit value assertion about the message or the owner, so a pass by itself does not guarantee that delivery would be safe or desirable. A message that fails is not necessarily associated with the author domain either, and some messages making authorized use of the domain can still fail, so a receiving organization may honour the owner's requested handling for failures but is not required to. DMARC is commonly one input to more complex filtering decisions.

DMARC also specifies a reporting framework, in companion documents. A receiving organization can generate regular reports about messages that use author domains for which a policy record exists, and send them to the addresses the owner asked for. Owners can use the reports, and especially the aggregate reports, not only to find sources of mail fraudulently using their domain but also to flag and fix gaps in their own authentication practices. A receiving organization supporting DMARC is under no obligation to send the reports, although it is recommended that they send aggregate reports.

The use of DMARC creates interoperability challenges that need consideration before deployment, particularly with configurations that can cause mail to be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: Two checks already exist for the sending domain. DMARC adds the missing piece: a way for the domain's owner to say that those two checks have to be tied to the domain in the From header, and to say what to do when they are not.

sections.title: Author Domain, Organizational Domain and Alignment
sections.content:
Several terms carry the weight of the mechanism. The author domain is the domain in the From header field. A DMARC policy record is the published record that describes the policy for a domain. The domain owner is the entity that controls a domain, and the domain owner assessment policy is the handling preference that the owner expresses for messages that fail validation. Enforcement is the state in which that preference is actually applied, as opposed to monitoring mode, in which it is only observed. The mail receiver is the organisation receiving the mail.

Two organisational terms matter for finding the right policy. The organizational domain of a domain is the domain at the top of the namespace hierarchy for that domain while having the same administrative authority as the domain, and it is determined by the tree walk described later. A public suffix domain is a domain that allows independent organisations to register their own subdomains, such as .com, .org, .us and .co.uk; the organisation managing one is a public suffix operator. For example, ietf.org is a registered domain name and .org is its public suffix domain.

Identifier alignment is the condition that has to hold for a pass. Two modes are defined. Relaxed alignment holds when the author domain has the same organisational domain as an authenticated identifier. Strict alignment holds when the author domain is identical to the authenticated identifier. The choice is the owner's, expressed in the policy record, and in practice nearly all owners have found relaxed alignment sufficient. Domain name comparisons in this context are case-insensitive.

The worked example in the RFC shows the three outcomes. An authenticated identifier of foo.example.com with an author domain of news.example.com is in relaxed alignment, because the two have the same organisational domain, example.com. An identifier of news.example.com with an author domain of news.example.com is in strict alignment, because the two are identical. An identifier of foo.example.net with an author domain of news.example.com has no alignment at all, because the two do not share a common organisational domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Alignment asks whether the domain that vouched for the message belongs to the same organisation as the domain claiming it. Two domains under example.com count as aligned; two under different registries do not.

sections.title: The DMARC Policy Record
sections.content:
A domain owner or public suffix operator advertises participation by publishing policy records. The records are stored as DNS text records with names starting with the label _dmarc. The owner of example.com would publish at _dmarc.example.com, and a receiver looking for the policy for mail with that author domain would issue a text query for that name. An owner can choose not to participate simply by not publishing a record. A record published at an organisational domain also applies to the subdomains under it, and the policy for those subdomains can be the same as the organisational domain's or different, depending on which values the record carries.

Using the DNS has the benefit of reusing an extremely well-established operations, administration and management infrastructure rather than creating a new one. A text record can comprise multiple character-string objects, and where it does, the module performing the evaluation must concatenate them in order and parse the result as a single string.

Records follow the extensible tag-value syntax used by DKIM. Only tags defined in the registry created by the document are processed, and unknown tags must be ignored. The v tag is required and must come first, and its only possible value is DMARC1; if it is not first, is absent, or has another value, the entire record must be ignored.

The p tag gives the handling preference for the domain itself and for its subdomains, unless the subdomain policies override it. Its values are none, where the owner expresses no preference; quarantine, where the owner considers the mail suspicious but it may still be valid; and reject, where the owner considers every failure clear evidence that the use of the domain name is not valid. If the tag is absent from an otherwise valid record, the record is treated as if it said p=none. The sp tag carries the same choices for existing subdomains, and the np tag for non-existent subdomains.

The adkim and aspf tags choose strict or relaxed alignment for the two underlying mechanisms, and both default to relaxed. The rua tag lists the addresses to which aggregate feedback reports are to be sent, and the ruf tag lists the addresses for message-specific failure reports. If either tag is absent, receivers must not generate that kind of report for the domain, and URIs using schemes the receiver does not support must be ignored. The fo tag gives the failure reporting options, and its content is ignored if no ruf tag is present.

The psd tag is a flag saying whether the domain is a public suffix domain, and the t tag is a test mode. With t=y the receiver is asked not to apply the policy but to apply any special handling it has, on the understanding that the policy applied to failing messages will be one level below the specified one, so a quarantine policy behaves like none and a reject policy behaves like quarantine.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is a short list of tag and value pairs. The version tag has to come first or the whole record is ignored. The policy tag says what to do with failures, and the reporting tags say where the owner wants to hear about them.

sections.title: Finding the Policy in the DNS
sections.content:
The organisational domain serves two purposes. The organisational domain of the author domain establishes the policy record for that domain when no record is published specifically for it. The organisational domains of an authenticated identifier and of the author domain are used in determining identifier alignment between the two.

The earlier specification defined the organisational domain as the domain registered with a registrar and discussed using a public suffix list as the authoritative list of parent domains, but it mandated no particular list and gave no guidance on how often receivers should refresh it. This update defines a discovery technique known as the DNS tree walk, which allows policy records to be published at several points in the namespace and suits organisations with decentralised DNS management.

The flexibility has a cost. Because the walk relies on the receiver making a series of DNS queries, an ill-intentioned domain owner could send mail with author domains carrying tens or hundreds of labels to mount a denial-of-service attack. A shortcut guards against this, so that author domains with more than eight labels do not result in more than eight DNS queries. Observed data at the time of publication showed domains with up to seven labels in use, so eight was chosen as the limit to allow for some future expansion of the namespace.

The steps are as follows. Query for a text record matching the policy record format at the starting point. Discard any record that does not start with a version tag identifying the current version of DMARC, and discard all of them if more than one is returned; if a single record remains and it carries a psd=n or psd=y tag, stop. Break the subject domain name into ordered labels, counting them from the right. If there are fewer than eight labels, remove the left-most label; if there are eight or more, remove labels until seven remain. Query again at the new target, apply the same discarding rules, remove one more label, and repeat until the process stops or no labels remain.

The example in the RFC uses the arbitrary author domain a.b.c.d.e.f.g.h.i.j.mail.example.com, which needs eight queries to find the policy record or organisational domain, starting at the full name and ending at _dmarc.com.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver looks for a record under the exact domain, then works upwards label by label until it finds one or runs out of name. The walk stops at eight queries at most, so a very long domain name cannot be used to flood the receiver with lookups.

sections.title: What a Receiving Mail Server Does
sections.content:
A receiver wishing to participate applies the mechanism to inbound messages when a policy record exists that applies to the author domain, and sends aggregate feedback reports to owners that request them. It might also send failure reports. The steps can take place during the SMTP transaction and should do so if the receiver plans to honour policies at the enforcement state.

The steps begin by extracting the author domain from the From header field, converting a U-label into an A-label for further processing. If zero or more than one domain is extracted, DMARC validation is not possible and the process terminates, although where more than one is retrieved the receiver may choose to go forward anyway. If exactly one author domain exists, the receiver performs policy discovery to determine whether the mechanism applies; if no record is discovered, the mechanism does not apply and validation terminates for that message.

Next, for each underlying authentication mechanism, the receiver performs the required check if it has not already been done, and preserves the results. For SPF the preserved results must include pass or fail, the reason for a failure if available, and the domain name used to complete the check. For DKIM signature validation, the results for each signature checked must include pass or fail, the reason for a failure if available, and the values of the d and s tags.

Alignment checks are then conducted where necessary, and the result determines a pass or a fail. The final handling of any message is always a matter of local policy and is left to the discretion of the receiver. A receiver may reject or quarantine a message even if it passes the check, because a pass says nothing about the message itself, and receivers are encouraged to keep anti-abuse technologies in place.

A receiver may accept mail that fails even where the published policy is reject. Because legitimate messages can fail for reasons DMARC cannot describe, and because rejecting can harm mailing lists, receivers should not reject messages solely because of a published policy of reject, but should apply other knowledge and analysis instead. Where a receiver deviates from a published policy, it should make the fact and the reason available to the owner through the PolicyOverride feature of the aggregate report. To enable owners to receive feedback without changing mail processing, a discovered policy of p=none must not modify existing handling processes.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver works out the domain, finds the policy, checks the signatures, and decides whether the sending domain belongs to the same organisation as the claiming one. The final decision on what to do with the message is the receiver's own, and the RFC advises against turning away mail purely because a policy says reject.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Both underlying authentication methods give some assurance that a message was transmitted by a mail transfer agent authorised to do so. SPF policies map domain names to sets of authorised servers, and a validated DKIM signature indicates that the message was sent by a server with access to a matching private key.

Whenever mail is sent there is a risk that an overly permissive source sends mail that receives a pass the domain owner did not intend. Such results can lead systems to treat a message as authentic, and they let an unauthorised sender evade the owner's intended handling for failures. To avoid this, no unauthorised source must be able to add DKIM signatures to the domain's mail or to send mail that evaluates as an SPF pass. If a domain owner wishes to include a permissive source in its SPF record, that source can be excluded from DMARC consideration by using the question-mark qualifier on the associated SPF record.

URIs published in DNS text records are well-understood targets for attack, because specifications expose email addresses that could be flooded, and common DNS names plainly identify where services can be found. Domain owners will need to harden these addresses against high-volume denial-of-service attacks, against deliberately malformed reports intended to find parsing or processing weaknesses, and against reports containing false claims, including the possibility of false data from a compromised but known receiver.

DMARC and its underlying mechanisms depend on the security of the DNS. An attacker who can snoop on DNS traffic learns who is receiving mail using the domain. An attacker who can block outgoing or reply DNS messages can prevent systems from discovering senders' policies. An attacker who can send forged response packets can make aligned mail appear unaligned, or the other way round. Signing records with DNSSEC lets recipients validate the integrity of the data and discard forged responses, and DNS over TLS or DNS over HTTPS can mitigate snooping and forged responses.

Display name attacks, where the display part of the From header carries a well-known name while the address is arbitrary, are increasingly common but are out of scope for DMARC. Messages that do not contain precisely one From domain are also out of scope, and that exposes an attack vector: an attacker can craft messages with several From domains, including the spoofed one, to bypass validation and have the message displayed with the spoofed domain shown to the victim. Where such messages are not rejected for other reasons, care must be taken to recognise them as the threats they might be.
sections.plainLanguage: The weaknesses come from the parts DMARC relies on. A too-permissive sending list lets a spoofer pass, the reporting addresses are visible targets, and the DNS can be tampered with. The RFC suggests signing the DNS and encrypting the lookups.

sections.title: Changes From the Earlier Version
sections.content:
The document records what changed from the earlier specification, which was informational rather than a standard. Several tags were added to the policy record format: np for the policy on non-existent domains, imported from the companion document on that subject; psd, a flag saying whether the domain is a public suffix domain; and t, which replaces some of the function of the removed percentage tag. Three tags were removed: pct, which asked for the policy to be applied to only a percentage of failing messages; rf, which specified the requested format of failure reports; and ri, which specified the requested interval between aggregate reports.

The removal of the percentage tag is explained in an appendix. The intent of that tag had been to let an owner move gradually from one policy to the next. Operational experience showed it was usually not applied accurately unless the value was either zero or one hundred, and the inaccuracies varied widely between implementations. The value zero took on unintended significance as a signal used by some intermediaries and mailbox providers to deviate from standard handling, usually by rewriting the From header field to avoid failures downstream. Those custom actions proved valuable, because a domain owner's aggregate reports could reveal how much of its traffic was routing through intermediaries that do not rewrite that field. Keeping the function but supporting a tag with only two valid values made little sense, so the new test tag takes its place, with values meant to be analogous to zero and one hundred.

Policy discovery and the determination of the organisational domain now use the tree walk rather than relying only on a public suffix list. The section on what a domain owner should do is greatly expanded, explaining not just what to do but why and what each decision costs, and it makes explicit that domains for general-purpose email should not deploy a policy of reject.
sections.plainLanguage: The main visible changes are new tags and the removal of old ones. The percentage tag went because receivers applied it inconsistently, and the tree walk replaces the reliance on a public suffix list.

viz.caption: The tags in a DMARC policy record

items.label: Version
items.desc: Required, and must be the first tag. The only possible value is DMARC1, and the whole record is ignored otherwise.

items.label: Policy
items.desc: What to do with mail that fails: none, quarantine or reject. Absent means none.

items.label: Subdomain policy
items.desc: The same three choices, for existing subdomains of the organizational domain.

items.label: Non-existent subdomain policy
items.desc: The same three choices, for subdomains that do not exist.

items.label: DKIM alignment
items.desc: Whether DKIM alignment must be strict or relaxed. Defaults to relaxed.

items.label: SPF alignment
items.desc: Whether SPF alignment must be strict or relaxed. Defaults to relaxed.

items.label: Aggregate report URIs
items.desc: Where to send the periodic summary of messages using the domain.

items.label: Failure report URIs
items.desc: Where to send per-message failure reports.

items.label: Failure options
items.desc: Which failure reports to generate. Ignored if there is no ruf tag.

items.label: Public suffix flag
items.desc: Whether the domain is a public suffix domain.

items.label: Test mode
items.desc: Signals that the policy should not be applied yet while the owner is testing it.

viz.caption: How the receiver finds the policy

items.title: Start at the author domain
items.text: Look for a policy record at the label _dmarc followed by the domain from the From header.

items.title: Then walk up
items.text: If nothing is found, drop the left-most label and look again, until no labels are left.

items.title: Eight queries at most
items.text: A domain with more than eight labels still results in no more than eight queries, so a long name cannot be used to flood the receiver.

items.title: Stop at a public suffix
items.text: A record with psd=n or psd=y ends the walk, because it marks the edge of one organisation's namespace.

viz.caption: The steps a receiving server takes, illustrative, not from the RFC

messages.label: Message
messages.note: The domain in the From header becomes the author domain.

messages.label: TXT query
messages.note: Look for a DMARC policy record, walking up the name if needed.

messages.label: Pass or fail
messages.note: Then the published policy decides what happens to the message.

items.title: Too permissive a source
items.text: An overly permissive source can send mail that passes DMARC without the owner intending it, which lets a sender escape the handling the owner asked for.

items.title: Reporting addresses are targets
items.text: Addresses published in DNS records can be flooded, so a domain owner has to harden them against denial of service and malformed reports.

items.title: The DNS has to be trusted
items.text: If an attacker can block or forge DNS answers, they can make aligned mail look unaligned. Signing the DNS and encrypting the lookups helps.

items.title: Display name attacks are out of scope
items.text: Putting a familiar name in the display part of the From header is not something DMARC addresses.

items.title: Messages with several From domains
items.text: Because such messages are outside the scope of the specification, an attacker can use them to bypass validation, so a receiver has to recognise them as threats.

items.title: A standard, not advice
items.text: The document moves from an informational status to a Standards Track one.

items.title: New tags
items.text: The np, psd and t tags were added.

items.title: Removed tags
items.text: The pct, rf and ri tags were removed.

items.title: The DNS tree walk
items.text: Policy discovery and the determination of the organizational domain now walk up the DNS rather than relying only on a public suffix list.

items.title: More guidance for owners
items.text: The section on what a domain owner should do is greatly expanded, including an explicit warning that general-purpose email domains should not deploy a policy of reject.
